CausalChain: Overexpression of circMAT2B -> Upregulation and maintenance of oncogenic PKM2 activity (via microRNA sponging and/or protein-protein interactions) -> Enhanced aerobic glycolysis and lactate production -> Acidification of tumor microenvironment stabilizes HIF-1α -> Promotion of angiogenesis, metastasis, and sorafenib resistance -> CRISPR-mediated inhibition of circMAT2B -> Shift from PKM2-dominance to PKM1-like activity, favoring oxidative phosphorylation -> Reduced lactate production -> Destabilization of HIF-1α -> Decreased angiogenesis and metastasis, leading to improved sorafenib sensitivity
Hypothesis: Inhibition of circMAT2B in hepatocellular carcinoma cells through CRISPR-based strategies will downregulate its regulation of oncogenic PKM2 activity (potentially mediated via microRNA sponging and altered protein interactions), resulting in a metabolic switch from aerobic glycolysis to enhanced oxidative phosphorylation. This metabolic reprogramming will lower lactate production, thereby reducing the stabilization of HIF-1α and its downstream effects on angiogenesis and metastasis, ultimately enhancing the tumor’s responsiveness to sorafenib. Implementation of advanced metabolic flux assays and multi-omics analyses will further elucidate the mechanistic underpinnings and validate the therapeutic efficacy of this approach.
Abstract: This study investigates a novel approach to reprogramming cancer metabolism in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by targeting the circular RNA circMAT2B using CRISPR-based inhibition. We hypothesize that precise downregulation of circMAT2B will attenuate its regulatory influence on oncogenic PKM2 activity—potentially mediated through disruption of microRNA sponging interactions—thereby shifting the cellular energy metabolism from aerobic glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation. This metabolic shift is expected to reduce lactate production, destabilize HIF-1α, and consequently suppress angiogenesis, metastasis, and resistance to sorafenib. By integrating state-of-the-art techniques such as CRISPR interference, Seahorse metabolic flux analysis, and multi-omics profiling, this work aims not only to validate the mechanistic cascade from circMAT2B inhibition to improved drug response but also to uncover any compensatory pathways that might undermine the therapeutic effect.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that inhibiting circMAT2B would reduce oncogenic PKM2 activity, shifting metabolism from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation, and thereby decrease lactate-mediated stabilization of HIF-1α leading to reduced angiogenesis, metastasis, and enhanced sorafenib sensitivity. The new hypothesis builds on this causal chain by: (1) explicitly incorporating a potential mechanism—disruption of microRNA sponging—that connects circMAT2B with PKM2 regulation; (2) employing contemporary CRISPR-based gene inhibition methods for precise targeting; (3) integrating advanced metabolic and multi-omics techniques to quantitatively monitor metabolic shifts and downstream effects; and (4) addressing potential compensatory pathways to strengthen the translational impact. Each revised step directly corresponds to the original steps: it begins with high circMAT2B expression enabling PKM2 oncogenic activity, continues through aerobic glycolysis and lactate production leading to HIF-1α stabilization, and culminates in a reversed cascade upon circMAT2B inhibition, resulting in therapeutic benefits.
